title: Example 18-8: Caret for Insertion of a Phrase

illustrates.quote:
a. When print includes inserted text preceded by a caret, the caret must be on the same line as the first word of the inserted text.
b. Enclose the insertion in braille grouping indicators. Note: the grouping indicators will likely require grade 1 indicators preceding them.
c. Ignore colored font attributes indicating text to be inserted.
d. List the caret symbol and the grouping indicators on the Special Symbols page, or explain them in a transcriber’s note before the text.

blocks.text: The insertion in the following sentence is preceded by a caret ^ and enclosed in braille grouping indicators.
The War of the Whiskers ^between France and England raged from 1152 to 1453.

print.notes: The inserted phrase "^between France and England" is printed in red — ignored per 18.6.5c. The braille grouping indicators (;< / ;>) that must enclose the inserted phrase cannot be produced (F-187, no such symbol exists anywhere in the codebase); built as plain inline text, so wording is still checkable even though the enclosure is not.

uncertain: Unresolved: the given braille's own note reads a REFERENCE form of the caret sign (".=@5") where forward-translating a plain mention of "^" in running prose produces bare "@5" (no ".=" prefix) — a UEB "symbol used as a reference, not a use" convention with no Emboss code path to invoke; not chased further since the file's own mismatch is already fully explained by F-187 (see differences.md §4).
resolution: Braille already agreed and re-extraction confirms it exactly; wording of both the note and the sentence confirmed by back-translation (the note’s own ".=@5" is the ordinary UEB caret sign, not a transcriber-defined symbol — F-188 does not apply to this note; only the ";<"/";>"  braille grouping indicator pair, F-187, is unrepresentable). illustrates rule narrowed to 18.6.5a (the caret-placement clause this example’s own braille directly exercises) with a-d quoted in full since b/c/d also apply.
